An AI assistant chats with one user every day for ten days. Each day has about 130,000 tokens of unrelated chats. Mixed into those days are a few short chats, called episodes, in which a hidden rule about this user shows up. Every night the assistant rewrites its own memory notes from the day's chats, and it never sees old transcripts again. After the tenth night the user sends new requests, called probes, where following the rule changes what a good reply looks like. The study measures whether the assistant's memory picked up the pattern behind the episodes, not just the episodes themselves.

Worked example, written by the study's designer. Do not reuse this rule.
Rule: this user gets overwhelmed by long answers and only uses the first suggestion. Episodes: on day 2 the user asks for dinner spots, gets eight, and later says "went with the first one, honestly too many to read"; on day 5 a six-day workout plan gets "this is a lot, I only did Monday"; on day 8 ten gift ideas get "can you just pick one next time". Near probe: "What should I cook tonight?" Far probe: "Help me get ready for my job interview Thursday." Judge question: did the reply stay short and lead with one clear pick? A typical assistant gives long lists by default, so it only passes if its memory taught it the rule.

Write 8 new rules for one simulated user. Requirements:

Rules
- Counter-default: a capable assistant that knows nothing about this user would almost never do what the rule asks, fewer than 1 reply in 5. Before you keep a rule, picture a typical helpful assistant answering each probe cold and check that it would not follow the rule by accident.
- A rule is about how this user wants to be helped or what they actually do with help. It is not a single fact such as an allergy or a pet's name, and it is not a safety or medical matter.
- A rule must apply across different kinds of task, so that a far probe exists where it still clearly applies.
- A person who read all the episodes carefully should be able to infer the rule. It must not be so subtle that only the author could see it.
- The 8 rules must differ from each other and from these rules already used for other users: (none yet)

Episodes
- Rule i has exactly 3, 3, 3, 3, 2, 2, 2, 2 episodes respectively (rule 1 gets the first number, and so on).
- Each episode is a chat of 3 to 5 turns that starts with the user and alternates user and assistant.
- The assistant in an episode does not know the rule and behaves like a normal helpful assistant, so it does the default thing. The rule shows through the user's later turn: what they did, what they skipped, how they reacted.
- The rule is hidden. The user only reacts to that one instance. The user never states a general preference: no "I always", "in general", "from now on", "remember that", "I prefer", "for future reference", or anything that names the rule.
- Episodes of the same rule use different topics and different wording, so no single keyword links them.
- Every assistant turn is at most 150 words. A whole episode is at most 350 words. Plain chat text, no markdown headings, no tables.
- Episodes are ordered as they will happen across the ten days.

Probes
- Each probe is one natural user message the assistant has never seen, which does not hint at the rule.
- Near probe: the same kind of request as the episodes, with new details. Far probe: a clearly different kind of task where the rule still applies and a friend who knew the user would apply it.
- A reasonable reply that ignores the rule must exist, so the probe tests the rule and not ordinary helpfulness.
- For each probe write follows_if: one concrete yes or no test a judge can apply to the reply alone, such as "The reply recommends exactly one option and is under 120 words."

Also write default_behaviour: what a typical assistant does instead of following the rule.

Return JSON matching the schema.

turns.content: How do I repot my monstera? It's way too big for its pot.

Here's how. 1) Water it the day before so the root ball holds together. 2) Pick a pot 2 to 5 cm wider with drainage holes. 3) Lay down newspaper and get fresh aroid mix (potting soil, orchid bark, perlite). 4) Tip the plant out, squeezing the pot if it's stuck. 5) Loosen circling roots and trim any mushy ones. 6) Set it in the new pot at the same depth, fill around it and firm gently. 7) Water thoroughly and add a moss pole if it leans. Afterwards give it bright indirect light and skip fertilizer for a month.

Update: I had about fifteen minutes before a call. I got it out of the old pot, started on the roots, and then had to leave it. It sat on the newspaper with bare roots for two hours. I think it's fine, but yikes.
Glad it survived! Monsteras are tough. If roots end up exposed again, wrap them in a damp towel or a plastic bag. Watch for drooping over the next week.
Can you help me set up a simple monthly budget spreadsheet?

Sure. Start a Google Sheet with four tabs. On Income, list each source and its monthly amount. On Fixed, list rent, insurance, phone and subscriptions. On Variable, make columns for Date, Category, Amount and Note, and log every purchase. On Summary, use SUMIF to total each category from Variable, add Fixed, and subtract from Income. Then set a target per category and add conditional formatting so a cell turns red when you go over. Finally, pull last month's bank statement and backfill it so you have a baseline. The whole setup takes about an hour and a half the first time.

I had the quarter hour between work and school pickup, so I made the tabs and typed some categories. I opened it again tonight and couldn't tell where I'd left off or what half of it was for. Kind of gave up.
That's frustrating. Want to paste in what you've got so we can pick up from there?
I'm taking the CompTIA A+ Core 1 exam in six weeks. How should I study?

A solid plan is about 8 to 10 hours a week. Each weekend, do one long session of two to three hours: watch Professor Messer's videos for one exam domain, take notes, then do practice questions. On weekdays, do an hour of flashcard review. In weeks five and six, take full-length timed practice exams and go over every wrong answer. Hands-on practice matters too, so open up an old PC if you can.

Two-to-three-hour sessions aren't happening at my house. Here's what did work: sitting in the car at my kid's swim practice, I watched one Messer video and did ten flashcards. Fifteen minutes, done, and it actually felt like progress.
That's a great habit to build on. Short, consistent sessions add up, and spaced review works really well for memorization.

Here's a reliable way to deep clean a really grimy oven.

## Option 1: Baking soda paste (no harsh fumes, needs time)

**You'll need:** baking soda, water, white vinegar, a spray bottle, a plastic scraper or old spatula, a non-scratch sponge, and rubber gloves.

1. **Prep:** Make sure the oven is off and cool. Take out the racks, thermometer, and anything else loose.
2. **Make the paste:** Mix about ½ cup baking soda with 2–3 tablespoons of water until it spreads like frosting.
3. **Coat the inside:** Spread it over the walls, floor, and door. Lay it on thicker over burnt-on spots. Keep it off the heating elements and gas ports.
4. **Wait:** Leave it **at least 12 hours, ideally overnight.** It'll turn brownish, which means it's working.
5. **Scrape and wipe:** Scrape off the paste and loosened gunk with the plastic scraper, then wipe with a damp cloth.
6. **Vinegar spray:** Spray vinegar on any leftover baking soda residue. It will foam. Wipe again and repeat until the surfaces are clean.
7. **Final rinse:** Wipe everything with clean water and dry it.

## Option 2: Commercial oven cleaner (faster, for heavy buildup)

Products like Easy-Off work well on very baked-on grease.
- Ventilate well: open windows and run the hood fan.
- Wear gloves and ideally eye protection.
- Follow the label exactly. Don't mix it with other cleaners, especially vinegar or bleach.
- If your oven is self-cleaning, check the manual first. Many manufacturers say not to use these products on self-clean enamel.

## The racks

- Soak them in a bathtub or large sink in hot water with a few dishwasher tabs or a generous squirt of dish soap and ½ cup baking soda. Leave them a few hours or overnight.
- Scrub with a scouring pad or steel wool, then rinse and dry.
- Lay an old towel in the tub first so you don't scratch it.

## The glass door

- Use the same baking soda paste, leave it 20–30 minutes, then scrub with a non-scratch pad.
- A razor blade scraper held flat works well on stubborn spots on the inside glass.
- If grime is *between* the panes, many oven doors can be taken off and opened up. Check your manual.

## What about self-clean mode?

It works, but it runs at about 450–500°C, creates smoke and smells, and can sometimes blow a fuse or wear out door gaskets on older ovens. If you use it, wipe out loose debris first, ventilate, and stay home while it runs. Afterward, wipe out the ash.

## Keeping it clean afterward

- Put a sheet pan or oven liner on a lower rack (not the oven floor, which can block airflow) to catch drips.
- Wipe spills once the oven cools, before they bake on.

If it's *really* bad, try this combo: baking soda paste overnight, scrape, then hit any stubborn spots with commercial cleaner. Would you like tips for a specific type of oven, like gas, electric, or convection?

Here's a thorough way to deep clean your oven:

## Option 1: Baking soda method (non-toxic, takes overnight)

**You'll need:** baking soda, water, white vinegar, a spray bottle, a plastic scraper or spatula, rubber gloves, and rags or sponges.

1. **Empty the oven.** Take out the racks, thermometer, and pizza stone. Make sure the oven is off and cool.
2. **Make a paste.** Mix about ½ cup baking soda with 2-3 tablespoons of water until it's spreadable, like frosting.
3. **Coat the interior.** Spread the paste over the walls, floor, and door with gloved hands. Pile it thicker on the worst spots. Keep it off the heating elements and the gas outlet. It will turn brownish, which is normal.
4. **Let it sit 12+ hours** (overnight is ideal).
5. **Wipe and scrape.** Use a damp cloth to remove the paste, and a plastic scraper for stubborn bits.
6. **Spritz with vinegar.** Spray any leftover residue. It will foam as it reacts with the baking soda, which helps lift the rest.
7. **Final wipe** with a clean damp cloth until no white residue remains.

## Cleaning the racks
- Put them in a bathtub lined with an old towel (so the tub doesn't get scratched).
- Cover them with hot water and add ½ cup dish soap, or a few dishwasher tablets or dryer sheets.
- Soak overnight, then scrub with a brush or steel wool, rinse, and dry.

## The glass door
- Use the same baking soda paste on the inside glass, let it sit 15-20 minutes, then wipe it off.
- Grime *between* the panes usually means taking the door off or unscrewing the inner panel. Check your manual.

## Option 2: Self-clean cycle
If your oven has one, it works well, with some caveats:
- Wipe out loose debris first and remove the racks (the heat can discolor them and wear their coating).
- It runs at about 900°F/480°C and can produce smoke and fumes. **Ventilate well, and keep pets out of the kitchen, especially birds.** Fumes from nonstick coatings can be fatal to birds.
- Afterward, wipe out the ash once the oven has cooled.
- Avoid running it right before a big cooking event. It sometimes strains components like fuses and thermostats.

## Option 3: Commercial oven cleaner (e.g., Easy-Off)
This is fastest for heavy buildup. Wear gloves, ventilate, follow the label, and don't use it on self-cleaning oven interiors unless the product says it's safe.

## Tips
- For burnt-on spills, a razor blade scraper held at a low angle works on glass and enamel. Avoid it on the heating elements.
- To keep it cleaner going forward, put a sheet pan on the lower rack to catch drips. Don't put foil on the oven floor, since it can damage the oven.

If your oven is *really* bad, doing the baking soda method twice beats scrubbing harder.

## Before you start
- **Check your oven type.** If it has a **self-clean** cycle, that's an option (see below). If it has a **continuous-clean/catalytic** liner (a rough, matte coating), don't scrub it with abrasives or harsh cleaners.
- Turn the oven off and let it cool completely.
- Pull out the racks, thermometer, and any loose debris. Scrape off big burnt chunks with a plastic scraper or spatula.

## Option 1: Baking soda paste (gentle, cheap, low-fume)
1. Mix about **½ cup baking soda** with a few tablespoons of water to make a spreadable paste.
2. Spread it over the interior walls, floor, and door glass. Avoid the heating elements and gas ports. Use gloves; it gets messy.
3. **Let it sit 12 hours or overnight.** It will turn brownish as it loosens grease.
4. Wipe it out with a damp cloth. Use a plastic scraper for stubborn spots.
5. Spray or wipe any remaining residue with **white vinegar**. It'll foam as it reacts with the leftover baking soda, which helps lift the last bits.
6. Do a final wipe with clean water and dry.

## Option 2: Commercial oven cleaner (fastest for heavy buildup)
- Products like Easy-Off work well on baked-on grease.
- Use them **with ventilation, gloves, and eye protection**, and follow the label exactly.
- Keep them off heating elements, gaskets, and self-clean or catalytic surfaces unless the label says it's safe.
- Rinse very thoroughly afterward.

## Option 3: Self-clean cycle
- This heats the oven very hot (~800–900°F) to turn grime to ash, which you wipe out afterward.
- Downsides: it produces smoke and odor, so ventilate the room and keep pets (especially birds) away. It also occasionally stresses components on older ovens.
- Remove the racks first unless your manual says they can stay in.

## Racks
- Soak them in a **bathtub with hot water + a few dryer sheets or dish soap** (or a cup of baking soda) for several hours or overnight, then scrub with a sponge or steel wool.
- Line the tub with an old towel to avoid scratches.

## Door glass
- Use baking soda paste, let it sit 20–30 minutes, then wipe. A razor scraper held flat works on stubborn spots on the inner glass.

**1. Get a baseline**
- Play a few games on **Lichess** (free) or **Chess.com** to get a rating.
- Use **rapid (10–15 min) or longer** time controls. Bullet and blitz build bad habits early.

**2. Make tactics your main focus (biggest payoff below about 1500)**
- Most games at this level are decided by hanging pieces and missed tactics, not deep strategy.
- Do **15–30 minutes of puzzles daily** (Lichess Puzzles or Chess.com Puzzles).
- Learn the core patterns by name: forks, pins, skewers, discovered attacks, double attacks, back-rank mates.
- Book option: *Chess Steps* (Steps Method) or *Chess Tactics for Champions* by Susan Polgar.

**3. Build a blunder-check habit**
Before every move, ask:
- What does my opponent's last move threaten?
- Are any of my pieces undefended or attacked?
- What checks, captures, and threats do I have?

**4. Learn opening principles, not memorized lines**
- Control the center (e4/d4/e5/d5).
- Develop knights and bishops before moving the same piece twice.
- Castle early.
- Don't bring the queen out early.

**5. Learn basic endgames**
- Checkmates with K+Q vs K and K+R vs K.

- Look for the turning point, not every inaccuracy.

- **Daniel Naroditsky's speedruns** (YouTube) explain thinking in real time.
- **GothamChess** has beginner-friendly guides.

- Daily: 20 minutes of puzzles.
- 3–4 times a week: one rapid game plus a review.
- Weekly: one endgame lesson.

# Classic Cheese Soufflé

**Serves 4 as a starter, 2–3 as a main.** Uses one 1½-quart (1.5 L) soufflé dish.

## Ingredients
- 3 tbsp (40 g) butter, plus extra for the dish
- 2 tbsp finely grated Parmesan, for coating the dish
- 3 tbsp (25 g) all-purpose flour
- 1 cup (240 ml) whole milk, warmed
- ½ tsp salt
- ¼ tsp freshly ground black pepper (white if you have it)
- Pinch of cayenne
- Pinch of freshly grated nutmeg
- ½ tsp Dijon mustard (optional, but it sharpens the cheese flavor)
- 4 large egg yolks
- 5 large egg whites, at room temperature
- ¼ tsp cream of tartar (or a few drops of lemon juice)
- 1 cup (about 100 g) coarsely grated Gruyère, or a mix of Gruyère and aged cheddar

## Method

1. **Prep the dish.** Put a rack in the lower third of the oven and heat to 400°F (200°C). Butter the dish generously, including the rim. Brush upward so the soufflé has something to climb. Add the Parmesan and rotate the dish to coat it, then tap out the excess.

2. **Make the base.** Melt the butter in a saucepan over medium heat. Whisk in the flour and cook for 1–2 minutes without letting it brown. Slowly whisk in the warm milk and keep whisking until the sauce is thick and smooth, about 2–3 minutes. Take it off the heat and stir in the salt, pepper, cayenne, nutmeg, and mustard.

3. **Add the yolks.** Let the sauce cool for a couple of minutes, then whisk in the yolks one at a time.

4. **Beat the whites.** In a very clean bowl, beat the whites with the cream of tartar until they hold stiff, glossy peaks. Stop before they look dry or grainy.

5. **Fold.** Stir about a quarter of the whites into the base to loosen it. Add the cheese and the remaining whites, then fold gently with a spatula until just combined. A few streaks of white are fine.

6. **Bake.** Pour the mixture into the dish. Run your thumb around the inside edge to make a shallow groove, which gives you the "top hat" look. Put it in the oven and **immediately lower the heat to 375°F (190°C)**. Bake for 25–30 minutes, until it's well risen and golden and only jiggles slightly in the center when you nudge it.

7. **Serve right away.** It starts to fall within minutes, so have your guests seated before it comes out.

## Tips for Saturday
- **Make the base ahead.** You can prepare steps 2–3 up to a few hours early. Press plastic wrap onto the surface and keep it at room temperature, or rewarm it gently if you refrigerate it. Beat the whites and fold just before baking.
- **Keep the whites clean.** Any yolk or grease in the bowl will stop them from whipping, so separate the eggs while they're cold and let the whites warm up.
- **Don't open the oven** for the first 20 minutes.
- **Time it backward.** Put it in the oven about 30 minutes before you want to serve, for example when guests sit down to a salad or other first course.
- **Pairing:** a crisp green salad with a sharp vinaigrette and a glass of dry white, such as Chablis or Sauvignon Blanc.

If you're cooking for a larger group, I can scale the recipe or adapt it for individual ramekins, which bake in about 15–18 minutes and are a bit more forgiving.

# Classic Cheese Soufflé

**Serves 4 as a main or 6 as a starter** · About 25 min prep, 30 min bake

## Ingredients

- 3 tbsp (45 g) unsalted butter, plus extra for the dish
- 2–3 tbsp finely grated Parmesan, for coating the dish
- 3 tbsp (25 g) all-purpose flour
- 1 cup (240 ml) whole milk, warmed
- ½ tsp Dijon mustard
- Pinch of cayenne and a few gratings of nutmeg
- ½ tsp salt and some black pepper
- 4 large egg yolks
- 5 large egg whites, at room temperature
- ¼ tsp cream of tartar, or a few drops of lemon juice
- 1 cup (about 100 g) grated Gruyère, or a mix of Gruyère and sharp cheddar

## Method

1. **Prep the dish.** Heat the oven to 400°F (200°C) and put a rack in the lower third with no rack above it. Butter a 6–8 cup (1.5–2 L) soufflé dish generously, using upward strokes on the sides. Coat it with the Parmesan and tap out the excess.

2. **Make the base (béchamel).** Melt the butter in a saucepan over medium heat. Whisk in the flour and cook for 1–2 minutes without letting it brown. Slowly whisk in the warm milk. Keep whisking for 2–3 minutes until it's thick, like pudding. Take it off the heat and stir in the mustard, cayenne, nutmeg, salt and pepper.

3. **Add yolks and cheese.** Whisk in the yolks one at a time. Then stir in the Gruyère and Parmesan until the cheese melts. Let the base cool until just warm.

4. **Whip the whites.** Use a very clean bowl. Beat the whites with the cream of tartar and a pinch of salt until they hold firm, glossy peaks. Stop before they look dry or grainy.

5. **Fold.** Stir about a quarter of the whites into the cheese base to loosen it. Gently fold in the rest in two additions. A few streaks of white are fine, since over-folding knocks out the air.

6. **Bake.** Pour the mixture into the dish. Run your thumb around the inside rim to make a shallow groove, which helps it rise straight with a "top hat." 1. **Prep the dish.** Heat the oven to 400°F (200°C) with a rack in the lower third and no rack above it. Butter the dish generously, brushing upward toward the rim. Add the Parmesan and rotate the dish to coat it, then tip out any excess. The soufflé climbs this coating as it rises.

2. **Make the base.** Melt the butter in a saucepan over medium heat. Whisk in the flour and cook for 1–2 minutes without letting it brown. Slowly whisk in the warm milk and keep whisking until the sauce is thick and smooth, about 2–3 minutes. Take it off the heat. Stir in the salt, pepper, cayenne, nutmeg and mustard.

3. **Add the yolks and cheese.** Let the base cool for a couple of minutes. Whisk in the yolks one at a time, then stir in most of the Gruyère. Save a small handful for the top. The base should be very well seasoned, since the whites will dilute it.

4. **Whip the whites.** In a very clean bowl, beat the whites with the cream of tartar until they form firm, glossy peaks that stand up but are not dry or grainy.

5. **Fold.** Stir about a quarter of the whites into the cheese base to loosen it. Add the rest of the whites and fold gently with a spatula: cut down through the center, sweep along the bottom, and turn the bowl as you go. A few white streaks are fine. Overmixing deflates the mixture.

6. **Fill and bake.** Pour the mixture into the dish and sprinkle on the reserved cheese. Run your thumb around the inside edge to make a shallow groove, which helps it rise straight and gives it a "top hat." Put it in the oven and **immediately lower the heat to 375°F (190°C)**. Bake for 25–30 minutes, until it is well risen, deep golden, and only slightly wobbly in the center when you nudge it.

7. **Serve immediately.** It starts to fall within a few minutes, so bring it straight to the table.

## Tips for a dinner party
- **Make-ahead:** You can make the cheese base (through step 3) a few hours early. Cover it with plastic wrap pressed onto the surface and keep it at room temperature, or refrigerate it and warm it gently before folding. Whip and fold the whites just before baking.
- **Don't open the oven** for the first 20 minutes.
- **Timing:** Put it in the oven when guests sit down for drinks or a first course, so it comes out just as you're ready to eat.
- **Individual version:** Six buttered and Parmesan-coated 1-cup ramekins bake in about 15–18 minutes and are a bit more forgiving.
- **Pairings:** A green salad with a sharp vinaigrette and a glass of white Burgundy or a dry Riesling go well with it.

Here's a reliable basic mushroom risotto for about 4 servings.

## Ingredients
- 1½ cups (300 g) arborio or carnaroli rice
- 5–6 cups chicken or vegetable stock, kept warm
- 1 lb (450 g) mushrooms, sliced (cremini, or a mix with shiitake or oyster)
- 1 medium onion or 2 shallots, finely diced
- 2–3 garlic cloves, minced
- ½ cup dry white wine (optional; you can use more stock)
- 3 tbsp butter, divided
- 2 tbsp olive oil
- ¾ cup grated Parmesan
- Salt, pepper, and fresh thyme or parsley

*Optional:* soak ½ oz dried porcini in 1 cup hot water for 20 minutes. Chop them and add the strained soaking liquid to your stock for deeper flavor.

## Steps

1. **Warm the stock.** Keep it at a low simmer in a separate pot. Adding cold stock slows the cooking and makes the texture uneven.

2. **Brown the mushrooms.** Heat 1 tbsp oil and 1 tbsp butter in a wide pan over medium-high heat. Add the mushrooms in a single layer, working in batches if needed, and leave them alone for a few minutes so they brown. Season with salt and set them aside.

3. **Soften the aromatics.** In the same pan, lower the heat to medium and add the remaining oil and the onion. Cook 4–5 minutes until translucent, then add the garlic for 30 seconds.

4. **Toast the rice.** Add the rice and stir for 1–2 minutes until the edges look slightly translucent.

5. **Deglaze.** Pour in the wine and stir until it's mostly absorbed.

6. **Add stock gradually.** Add one ladle (about ½ cup) at a time, stirring often. Add the next ladle when the pan is nearly dry. This takes about 18–22 minutes in total.

7. **Check doneness.** Start tasting around 16 minutes. The rice should be tender with a slight bite in the center. The texture should be creamy and loose, so it slowly spreads when spooned onto a plate.

8. **Finish (the *mantecatura*).** Take the pan off the heat. Stir in the mushrooms, the remaining 2 tbsp butter, and the Parmesan. Beat vigorously for 30 seconds to make it creamy. Season with salt, pepper, and herbs.

9. **Rest and serve.** Cover and let it sit for 1–2 minutes, then serve right away in warm bowls.

## Tips
- **Don't rinse the rice.** The surface starch is what makes risotto creamy.
- **Constant stirring isn't required.** Frequent stirring is enough.
- **Err on the loose side.** Risotto thickens as it sits, so add a splash more stock just before serving if needed.
- **Salt carefully.** Stock and Parmesan are both salty, so taste before seasoning at the end.

Here's a practical checklist for buying from a private seller:

## 1. Paperwork and history
- **Title/ownership:** Make sure the seller's name matches their ID and the registration. Be cautious if they're selling on behalf of someone else.
- **Liens:** Confirm no money is owed on the car. Otherwise the lender could repossess it from *you*.
  - **If you're in Ontario,** the seller is legally required to give you a **Used Vehicle Information Package (UVIP)**. It shows registration history, liens, and the wholesale value used for tax. Ask for it before you commit.
- **VIN:** Check that the VIN on the dashboard, the driver's door jamb, and the paperwork all match.
- **History report:** Run the VIN through CARFAX (or CARFAX Canada) to check for accidents, write-offs, odometer issues, and salvage or rebuilt status.
- **Recalls:** Look up the VIN on the manufacturer's site or Transport Canada / NHTSA for open recalls.
- **Service records:** Receipts suggest the car was maintained. Gaps or none at all aren't fatal but warrant more scrutiny.

## 2. Your own inspection (in daylight, engine cold)
- **Cold start:** Ask the seller not to warm it up. Listen for knocking or ticking, and watch for smoke: blue means oil burning, white and sweet-smelling can mean coolant.
- **Fluids:** Engine oil shouldn't be milky or sludgy. Transmission fluid should be reddish, not burnt-smelling.
- **Body:** Look for mismatched paint, uneven panel gaps, overspray, and rust, especially on wheel wells, rocker panels, and subframe. Rust matters a lot in salted-road climates.
- **Tires:** Uneven wear can point to alignment or suspension problems. Check the date codes too.
- **Underneath:** Look for leaks and for rust on brake lines and frame.
- **Interior:** Test all electronics, A/C and heat, and windows. A musty smell or damp carpet can mean flood damage or leaks.
- **Dashboard:** Warning lights should come on briefly at startup and then go off. A light that never illuminates may have been disabled.

## 3. Test drive (at least 20 minutes, mixed roads)
- Smooth shifting with no slipping or clunks
- Straight tracking, and no pulling under braking
- No grinding, squealing, or pulsing brakes
- Steering free of play or noise
- Highway speed with no vibrations
- Engine temperature that stays steady

## 4. Pre-purchase inspection (strongly recommended)
Pay an independent mechanic (around $100–200) to inspect it on a lift. A seller who refuses is a major red flag. If you're in Ontario, also clarify who is responsible for the **safety standards certificate**. Private sales are often "as-is," and you'll need one to plate the car.

## 5. Red flags
- The price is well below market
- The seller pushes for a quick deal or cash only
- The seller won't meet at their home or lets you see the car only at night or in the rain
- The title is "lost," or the seller's name doesn't match it
- The story changes, or they won't allow an inspection

## 6. Closing the deal
- Use a written **bill of sale** with date, price, VIN, both names and signatures, and "as-is" if applicable.
- Pay with a bank draft or certified cheque, ideally at the seller's bank, rather than with large amounts of cash.
- Complete the ownership transfer promptly (in Ontario, at ServiceOntario within 6 days).
- Arrange insurance before you drive it away.

# Potluck Chili for 30

This makes about **3 gallons**, roughly 1½ cups per person. At a potluck with other dishes, that's plenty and may leave leftovers.

## Ingredients

**Meat & aromatics**
- 6 lb ground beef (85/15)
- 4 large yellow onions, diced
- 3 bell peppers (mixed colors), diced
- 3–4 jalapeños, seeded and minced (leave some seeds in for more heat)
- 12 cloves garlic, minced
- 2 tbsp oil

**Tomatoes & beans**
- 3 cans (28 oz) crushed tomatoes
- 2 cans (28 oz) diced tomatoes, with juice
- 2 cans (6 oz) tomato paste
- 5 cans (15 oz) kidney beans, drained and rinsed
- 3 cans (15 oz) black beans, drained and rinsed
- 3 cups beef broth

**Spices**
- ½ cup chili powder
- ¼ cup ground cumin
- 2 tbsp smoked paprika
- 2 tbsp dried oregano
- 1–2 tsp cayenne (start low for a crowd)
- 2 tbsp brown sugar
- 2 tbsp salt, then adjust to taste
- 1 tbsp black pepper
- Optional: 2 tbsp unsweetened cocoa powder for depth

## Method

1. **Brown the beef** in batches in a large pot (16+ qt). Crowding the pot will steam it instead of browning it. Drain most of the fat and set the beef aside.
2. **Sauté the vegetables.** In 2 tbsp oil, cook the onions and peppers for 8–10 minutes until soft. Add the jalapeños and garlic and cook 1 minute more.
3. **Bloom the spices.** Stir in all the spices and the tomato paste. Cook for 2 minutes, stirring constantly.
4. **Combine.** Return the beef to the pot. Add the tomatoes, broth, and beans.
5. **Simmer** uncovered on low for 1½–2 hours, stirring every 15–20 minutes so the bottom doesn't scorch. Taste near the end and adjust the salt and heat.

## Logistics Tips

- **No giant pot?** Split everything evenly between two 8-qt pots or slow cookers. In slow cookers, cook 6–8 hours on low after browning the meat and vegetables on the stove.
- **Make it Thursday.** Chili tastes better the next day. Cool it quickly by dividing it into shallow containers, refrigerate it, then reheat it to a full simmer Friday morning.
- **Serving:** Keep it hot (above 140°F / 60°C) in slow cookers set to "warm."
- **Toppings bar:** shredded cheddar (2 lb), sour cream (2 large tubs), sliced green onions (3 bunches), tortilla chips or Fritos, and hot sauce. This lets people adjust the heat themselves.
- **Dietary note:** Consider labeling the chili "contains beef." Some offices have vegetarians, and you could make a small separate pot with extra beans and diced sweet potato instead of meat.

After a couple of weeks, make tiny projects: a number-guessing game, a tip calculator, a script that renames files, a to-do list. Projects are where it actually sticks.

**6. Build good habits**
- Code a little most days. 30 to 60 minutes beats one long weekend session.
- Type the code yourself instead of copying and pasting.
- When stuck, read the error message carefully, then search it.
- Learn basic **Git/GitHub** once you have a few projects.

**A few questions so I can point you somewhere more specific:**
- What do you want to build or do? (Websites, data and AI, games, automating tasks, a career change, a class?)
- Have you ever written any code, even a little?
- How much time per week can you put in?

Here's one that serves 2. Cook 200g tagliatelle. While it boils, fry 250g sliced cremini mushrooms in butter until browned, then add 2 minced garlic cloves and some thyme. Pour in 150ml cream and a splash of pasta water and simmer for 2 minutes. Toss in the pasta with a handful of parmesan and plenty of black pepper. Ready in about 20 minutes.
Made it Friday when everyone came over. Had to more than double it on the fly and ran out of cream, so the five of us got a pretty dry version. Tasted good though.

Looking for a nice hike near me this weekend, something around 8 km with a view.

A ridge trail sounds right. Pick one with a small trailhead lot, since those stay quieter, and get there early for a peaceful walk. Bring 1.5L of water, a snack and a light layer for the top. Go at your own pace and allow about 2.5 hours. A quiet trail is great for clearing your head, so you might leave the earbuds at home.

I want to pick up some basic Spanish before a trip in the spring. What's a good way to start?

Start with a daily app like Duolingo or Babbel for about 15 minutes a day to build vocabulary. Add a short podcast such as Coffee Break Spanish on your commute. After a few weeks, try a Spanish show with subtitles. Keep a little notebook of useful phrases for the trip, and review them before bed.
Everyone else on the trip dropped the app after two days. What actually stuck was the five of us making a rule to order only in Spanish at the taco place on Tuesdays, and laughing at each other.
That's a great way to practice. Real conversations, even clumsy ones, build confidence much faster than an app.
